# Introduction

This assignment is to be completed in groups of 4-5. Further, all students in your group need to be assigned to the same R tutorial group (Friday's tutorial). You can sign yourself up for a group on Canvas. Please do so \textbf{before the start of your first R tutorial on Friday September 4th.} You can use the Discussion Board in Canvas if you do not have a group yet or if your group is incomplete.

The assignment has 5 parts, and each part corresponds to the course material of that week (with the exclusion of week 6, for which there is no R programming material). 

You are supposed to hand in these assignments on Canvas at the following dates:

  - **Deadline 1** *Sunday September 27th, at 23:59pm*: you are supposed to hand in weeks 1, 2, and 3 of this assignment.   This will determine 18\% of your overall course grade
  - **Deadline 2** *Sunday October 11th, at 23:59pm*: you are supposed to hand in weeks 4, and 5 of this assignment. This will determine 12\% of your overall course grade 

The R tutorials (each Friday) will consist of two halves. During the first half, you will discuss the tutorial exercises. These can be downloaded separately from Canvas. During the second half, you can work on this graded assignment within your own group. The purpose is that you find out how to work with R for doing statistical analyses by yourself. The tutorial exercises are meant to teach you basic commands to get you started, but to answer the problem sets in this assignment, you might need to research your own solutions, and use functions and commands not described in the tutorial exercises. Learning how to solve your own research problems is integral part of learning R. When you and your group get stuck on how to approach an exercise, the hierarchy in finding your way is as follows:

-	use the concepts from the tutorial exercises;
- use the cheat sheets available on Canvas;
-	use Google, YouTube, StackOverflow, or another website;
- ask the teacher.

The use of generative AI is \textbf{not} permitted and may result in a grade of 0. See the AI protocol in the course manual for details.

To answer the assignment, you can simply fill out this R markdown document. There are designated places which you can fill with R code. There are also designated spaces for you to answer each question. Often, the structure of an answer will be as follows. First, you type the R code in the designated box. This will show how you analyzed the data to get the answer to the question. Below the box for the R code, you will then summarize your answer to the question, i.e. what are the conclusions that you draw from the data analysis? 

When handing in, you are supposed to submit this .Rmd file, and a knitted version of this document. You can knit this document to pdf, word, or html. Knitting to pdf requires you to have a .tex distribution installed on your computer. Knitting to Word requires you to have Word installed. 

The exercises are designed such that you should be able to finish the majority of them during the tutorial each week. If you are not able to finish them fully during that time, you are expected to work on it in your own time using the computers on campus or your own device. It is best to meet as a group in-person when working together. If you want to work remotely, github is a good platform to guarantee smooth collaboration. Alternatively, you can email this .Rmd file back and forth to one another as a group, but this is not recommended as it is more cumbersome.

We encourage you to keep your code blocks, printing statements, and final answers, as short as possible. In any case, there is a page limit of 6 pages per week, which encompasses the total length of this document which consists of the questions, your coding lines, and your answers. When your answers to questions of the respective week exceed this page limit, they will not be graded, resulting in zero points.

Each week consists of 1, 2, or 3 subquestions. The total amount of points you can earn per week is 20 points. 

# Week 1 

1.  Find the dataset “movies3.tsv” on Canvas. Describe your data set: How many observations does it have. How many variables are there? How many subjects? What consists of a subject? \textbf{[4 points]}

```{r}
movies <- read.delim("movies3.tsv")
dim(movies)
```

**Your Answer:**

Based on the (dim) output, the dataset has 707 observations and 19 variables. Each row represents a specific movie, meaning that there are 707 subjects in total. A subject in this specific context is simply the movie itself. 

2. Which of the following types of variables are present in your data set? (i) nominal; (ii) ordinal; (iii); interval; (iv) ratio. If present, name one example of such a variable present in your data set.  \textbf{[4 points]} 

```{r}
str(movies)
```

**Your Answer:**

(i) Genre or original_language, since these represent categories without any numerical order.
(ii) There are no strictly ordinal variables present in this dataset. 
(iii) Release_year, because the difference between years is mathematically meaningful, however there is no "true zero", as the year 0 does not reflect absence of time. 
(iv) Budget, revenue, and runtime. Because these are continuous numerical values where a true zero suggest zero dollars or zero minutes. 


3. A movie studio wants to know which types of movies are best at generating profit. The measure they use for this is the profitability ratio, which is defined as $$PR=\frac{Revenue}{Budget}.$$ Perform the following steps to provide the movie studio with an analysis which corresponds to their request:

a. Create the variable PR as the revenue of a movie divided by its budget. Report its mean, median, maximum, and minimum.  \textbf{[2 points]}
b. As you can probably see from your answer in a.), some movies have a PR of "Inf". What does this mean? Why are some movies assigned this value? \textbf{[2 points]}
c. As you can probably see from your answer in a.), some movies have a PR of "NA". What does this mean? Why are some movies assigned this value? \textbf{[2 points]}
d. For the movies that have a PR of "Inf", set its PR to "NA". After doing this, report the mean, median, maximum, and minimum of PR. How do you interpret the mean? \textbf{[2 points]}
e. What does a PR of at least one mean? What is the fraction of movies that have a PR of at least one? \textbf{[2 points]}
f. Create a boxplot of the variable PR. Make sure it has an appropriate title, and appropriate titles and labels for the x- and y-axis. Describe the shape of the boxplot. Give $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$ and $Q_4$. What does this tell you about the nature of making money in the movies industry? \textbf{[2 points]}
 
For each step, you should provide first all the code you used to answer the question and then formulate an answer using full sentences.

*Step a*

```{r}
movies$PR <- movies$revenue / movies$budget
mean(movies$PR, na.rm = TRUE)
median(movies$PR, na.rm = TRUE)
max(movies$PR, na.rm = TRUE)
min(movies$PR, na.rm = TRUE)
```

**Your Answer:**

The mean PR is Inf (infinity) and the median is 1.665002. The maximum PR is also Inf, and thrminimum PR is 0.

*Step b*

```{r}

movies[is.infinite(movies$PR), c("title", "budget", "revenue", "PR")]

```

**Your Answer:**

An "Inf" value means that the formula tried to divide a positive number by zero. By looking at the data, this happens as some movies have a recorded budget of 0, but a positive revenue. It is important to note that this does not mean that there was zero production cost, it just means that the budget data ismissing and was incorrecntly entered into the dataset as a zero. 

*Step c*

```{r}

movies[is.na(movies$PR), c("title", "budget", "revenue", "PR")]

```

**Your Answer:**

"NA" stands for Not Available. This outcome happens when R tries to divide zero by zero, which yields NaN (a type of NA). This correctly reflects these specific movies where both budget and revenue were recorded as a zero. 

*Step d*

```{r}

movies$PR[is.infinite(movies$PR)] <- NA
mean(movies$PR, na.rm = TRUE)
median(movies$PR, na.rm = TRUE)
max(movies$PR, na.rm = TRUE)
min(movies$PR, na.rm = TRUE)

```

**Your Answer:**

After replacing the infinite values with NAs, the new mean PR is 1813.041, the median is 1.55807, the max is 1,000,000, and the min is 0. 

The mean of 1,813 suggests that the average movie makes over 1,800 times its budget. However, by observing how far the mean is pulled away from the median, we can conculde that the mean is massively distorted by some extreme outliers and is not a fully reliable measure of a movie¨s performance. 

*Step e*

```{r}

mean(movies$PR >= 1, na.rm = TRUE)

```

**Your Answer:**

A PR of 1 or higher implies that the movie reached break-even or turned a profit. In this sample, approximately 60.36% of the movies achieved this. 

*Step f*

```{r}

boxplot(movies$PR,
        main = "Profitability Ratio of Movies",
        xlab = "Movies",
        ylab = "Profitability Ratio (Revenue / Budget)")
quantile(movies$PR,
          probs = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1),
          na.rm = TRUE)

```

**Your Answer:**

The boxplot is heavily right-skewed. Essentially all is compressed into a flat line at the bottom near zero, but there is at least one extreme outlier pulling the plot scale up to 1,000,000.
